isomorphs.claim: Insertion, Mark, Superscript, Subscript and Strikethrough are delimiter runs opened and closed by a repeated byte, and the same scanner disambiguates the one-byte and two-byte spellings. CommonMark emphasis and strong are that scan with a different byte, so the isomorph builds the same tree over the same spans.

An inline comment is a leaf opened and closed by a two-byte run whose body is taken literally rather than parsed as inline. A two-backtick code span is exactly that shape, which is why the pair holds and why pairing a comment with strong emphasis does not: strong parses its body.

An inline formula is a leaf opened and closed by a one-byte run whose body is taken literally; a one-backtick code span is the same shape. Formula additionally records which spelling opened it in `mode`, which is that kind's own business rather than a difference in what was built, and is named here so the exception is visible rather than assumed.

referenceless.anchor: Neither reference derives or stores a per-block identifier. A tree carrying one is not the tree either reference built, however CommonMark the syntax that produced it was -- so a case that carries this field has no same-job ratio against a reference and is reported as a bound, unless the corpus pairs it with a document that puts the same declaration in front of the reference. Declared per case and checked against the parser's dump in both directions, because the failure this closes was exactly a case whose syntax was CommonMark and whose tree was not.

logicalIsomorphs.claim: An explicit anchor DECLARES a name and binds it to the block it sits on; a link reference definition declares a name and binds it to a target. Same grammar shape -- one block, one name-to-target binding -- and the same subsequent operation at the level of the language: the name becomes addressable, so `[[Note#^id]]` resolves the one and `[id]` resolves the other. Both are read off the grammars. What each implementation then DOES behind that binding -- when it allocates, what it defers, what it skips -- is not part of the pairing; it is the thing being measured, and a pair rewritten until both engines run the same machinery would read 1.00x and measure nothing. DERIVED anchors are deliberately not paired: a heading whose anchor comes from its own text declares nothing, there is no name in the source to bind, and CommonMark has no production that derives one -- so block-heading has no isomorph and is reported as a bound. The two spellings differ in length, so the pair is generated to an equal COUNT of declarations rather than to equal bytes, and each name is indexed so both sides bind the same number of distinct identifiers.

A specimen definition and a GFM footnote definition are the same production: a one-line opener carrying a label, block content the opener owns, and a node that leaves ordinary document content for a side list the document holds -- Document.specimens against Document.footnotes, in both specs' own words. Each unit also carries a REFERENCE on both sides, for two reasons. First, the grammars differ on an unreferenced definition: this dialect keeps a specimen nobody cites, GFM DISCARDS a footnote nobody calls, so without the call the reference side parsed to nothing and the denominator was cmark-gfm throwing text away. Second, the reference must be the PARENTHESIZED form. specimens.md gives two reference forms and they are different productions: `(@label)` is a fixed delimiter pair around a sigil and a raw label, which is the GFM footnote call's shape with a different terminal, while the BARE `@label` is an unbracketed word-boundary trigger -- the autolink shape, paired separately as pair-cite. Pairing the bare form against a bracketed `[^label]` call matched the definitions and mismatched the calls.

A task marker is one Unicode scalar in brackets at the start of a list item's content, removed from the content and stored on the item. GFM's task list item is that production with the scalar restricted to a space or `x`; this dialect keeps the authored scalar instead of mapping it. Same production, one terminal wider -- which is what makes this pair, and what it measures. Both sides build ListItem, so an equal count proves nothing on its own; the pair names `marker` and the audit requires every item on BOTH sides to carry one, because an item whose marker went unread is still a list item. The reference is cmark-gfm.

A bracketed span and an inline link are the same production: an opening bracket, a body parsed as inline content, a closing bracket, and an immediately following paired-delimiter suffix taken raw and decoded into fields of the one node the production builds. The dialect spec says so directly -- a span is decided in the same bracket alternation as a link, and a valid link wins the position -- so the two are alternatives at one point in the grammar and not merely alike. The suffix is where they differ and nothing else is: `{.c}` decodes into attributes, `(/c)` decodes into a destination. Neither looks anything up. The two spellings are the same length here, so the pair is byte for byte as well as count for count.

A cross link and an empty-text inline link are the same production: fixed bracket delimiters around a body that is NOT parsed as inline, producing one leaf node that stores the body as a destination and has no children. Neither resolves it -- the cross-link spec is explicit that the parser stores the strings and the application finds the resource, and an inline link's destination is likewise stored, not looked up -- so the subsequent operation matches too. The empty text is deliberate: a cross link has no inline body, and pairing it against a link that did have one would hand the reference an inline parse this side never performs. Not the same length, so the pair is generated to an equal COUNT.

A bare citation key and a GFM `www.` autolink are the same production: an UNBRACKETED recognition triggered by a literal prefix at a word boundary, consuming a raw run bounded by a character class, producing one inline that stores the run without parsing it as inline and without resolving it. Both specs state the boundary condition in the same terms -- a citation opener must follow a scalar that is not a letter, number or underscore, so `foo@bar` is not one, and the `www.` form needs an eligible boundary -- and both state that nothing is looked up: the parser does not resolve bibliography keys, and an autolink's destination is stored. That shared shape is what makes the pair; scanning ordinary text for a trigger is the grammatical feature being measured, which is why this pairs with an unbracketed autolink rather than with a delimited `<...>` one. How many NODES each side materialises for that production -- one Link over a Text here, a Cite over a Citation with two affix slots there -- is emphatically not part of the pairing. It is the measurement, and refusing the pair over it would be designing the corpus by reading the implementations, which drives every ratio to 1.00x.

A block formula and a fenced code block are the same production: a LEAF block opened and closed by a run of one repeated character, whose body is taken LITERALLY rather than parsed, producing one node that carries the body as a literal and has no children. Same shape, different terminal -- the `$x$` against `` `x` `` rule, lifted to the block level, and the inline halves of exactly this pair are already held by substitution as pair-formula. The two fences are two and three characters long, so this half cannot be a byte-for-byte substitution and is generated to an equal COUNT of blocks.

A cross embed and an image are the same production: a `!` sigil immediately before a bracket-delimited destination that is NOT parsed as inline content, producing one leaf inline that stores the destination and has no children. The alt text is deliberately empty on the reference side -- a cross embed has no inline body, so an image that carried one would hand the reference an inline parse this side never performs, and with it empty both sides build a childless leaf. Neither resolves the destination: the cross-link spec says the parser stores the strings and the application finds the resource, and an image's destination is likewise stored. Not the same length, so the pair is generated to an equal COUNT.

A simple table and a GFM pipe table are the same production: a header line, a separator line that fixes the columns, body rows, terminated by a blank line, and CELLS THAT HOLD INLINES. tables.md says so three times for the simple form -- 'inline content in its cells', 'Segments are trimmed before inline parsing', and the explicit statement that block openers do not fire inside one, so 'heading, quote, and fence-looking lines remain inline cell text'. Only the cell separator differs: a column POSITION established by the dash-run line against a `|` scalar. The spec adds that all four table spellings 'produce the same Table model' and that 'the AST does not store a separate table kind for each spelling'. THIS CORRECTS A RECORDED REASON: the bounds table refused every table flavour on the ground that a grid cell holds a paragraph where a pipe cell holds inlines. That is true of the GRID table and of nothing else, and it was applied to the simple table without checking.

A block comment and a fenced code block are the same production: an opening delimiter line with zero to three leading spaces after container prefixes and only whitespace after the marker, a body kept LITERAL and not parsed as Markdown, and a closing delimiter line of the same marker within the same container; either can interrupt a paragraph. comments.md calls them 'Fences' in its own words. Same shape, different terminal -- `%%` against a run of three or more backticks -- which is the `$x$` against `` `x` `` rule at block level. It cannot be a substitution: mapping `%` to a backtick turns the two-byte line into a two-backtick run, which is not a fence at all, so the pair is sized by count. The INLINE comment is a separate production and is paired separately, by substitution, as pair-comment.

A fence whose info string is exactly `formula` is a formula block, and formulas.md and code.md both say so; every other info string keeps ordinary code-block behaviour. So this is not a production of the same SHAPE as a code fence, it IS the code fence production with one token changed, which makes it the narrowest pair in the corpus and a deliberate one: the fence scanner is held byte for byte identical and the only thing that varies is the info-string comparison and the routing of the finished leaf to a different kind. It measures none of the `$$` delimiter-line grammar, which is a separate production paired separately as pair-formulablock.

A properties envelope and a fenced code block are the same production: a leaf block opened and closed by a delimiter line, whose body is NOT parsed as Markdown. Same shape, different terminal -- `---` against a run of three or more backticks. What each does with the body afterwards, decode it into named fields or keep it literal, is the measurement and not part of the pairing. This pair is shaped unlike every other one in the corpus and deliberately so: properties.md says only one envelope is recognised, at the document's start, so the workload CANNOT scale by repeating the construct. It scales by the member lines inside a single envelope, which is why both sides carry a head and a tail and why `units` counts lines here rather than constructs. The earlier refusal -- once per document, no count to scale -- mistook the construct for the dimension.

A leaf directive and an ATX heading are the same production: a LEAF block recognised by a marker run at the start of its single line, the marker consumed into a FIELD, and the rest of the line parsed as INLINES owned by the block. `##` becomes level=2 and `::note` becomes name="note"; what follows is inline content either way. That the dialect hangs those inlines under a DirectiveLabel group where the heading holds them directly is node materialisation, which is never grounds to refuse. This pair publishes SAME-JOB ONLY. The isomorph half is a heading, and this dialect derives an anchor on every heading where neither reference does, so the isomorph's tree carries a field no reference builds -- which lands in twinCore, inflating Grammar's denominator and Shape's numerator while cancelling out of same-job. The corpus states that derivation under `unpairable`, the twin declares the field it carries, and the driver suppresses the two contaminated columns rather than printing them low and high. The dialect half derives nothing: a leaf directive's anchor is null.

A container directive and a block quote are the same production: a CONTAINER BLOCK -- a start condition, a per-line continuation condition, and contents parsed as BLOCKS. CommonMark defines that category itself and puts the block quote and the list item in it; the container directive is a third member of it. What differs is which continuation condition: a block quote continues while its lines carry the marker, a directive continues until its closing fence. That is the thing being measured. The pair counts Paragraph alongside the container because block parsing of the contents is the second half of the criterion and 50 against 50 per 50 units is what shows it matches. The earlier refusal said CommonMark's only FENCE opens a leaf, which compares the fence construct rather than the container production -- the reference here is not the fenced code block, it is the block quote. What the reader should discount for: a fenced container spends two delimiter lines per unit where a prefix container spends none, so at equal COUNT the dialect document is about three times the lines. That is the cost of the grammar rather than a hidden inequality, and it is why the pair is sized by count and says so.

A callout marker and a GFM task marker are the same production: a bracketed token at the START of a container's first line, taken out of the content and kept as a FIELD, with the rest of that line parsed as inlines owned by the container. `[!note]` on a block quote's first line becomes the callout's variant; `[x]` on a list item's first line becomes the item's marker. Counting alone would prove nothing here, because a callout whose `[!note]` went unread is still a block quote and a list item whose `[x]` went unread is still a list item -- so the pair names the binding on BOTH sides, each under the field name its own kind uses, and the audit checks that every node of the counted kind carries it. That the dialect puts the remaining inlines in a Title group where the list item wraps them in a Paragraph is node materialisation, which is never grounds to refuse. Without this pair the dialect callout form was a bound: its syntax is a CommonMark block quote and its tree is not, so a reference on the same bytes built a different tree.

A headerless simple table and a GFM pipe table are the same ROW production: a line cut into K ranges, each range's content parsed as INLINES, repeated for as many lines as the table holds. The cut is positional in one grammar and delimited in the other, which is the difference being measured; the subsequent operation is the same on both sides, and the pair counts TableRow alongside TableCell so that both halves of the criterion are checked rather than only the second. Where the two grammars genuinely differ is that GFM DESIGNATES its first row the head and the simple table's headerless form leaves every row in the body -- a destination for a row already parsed, not a different production, which is why both sides carry one extra row so that the same number of LINES becomes the same number of cells. The earlier refusal argued from GFM's table REQUIRING a header, which is a fact about the reference's table rather than about its row-and-cell production. Held by the absence of Paragraph: both spellings collapse into one the moment the table stops being recognised, and with an index that gains a digit the collapse would be silent, so both sides use the zero-padded form.

A grid table cell and a loose list item are the same production: a per-line POSITIONAL cut at a width established by an earlier line, whose joined remainders are then parsed as BLOCKS. A list item establishes its indent width from its own marker and strips that width off every following line; a grid cell takes the range between two column positions established by the border line and strips it off every line of the row. Both then parse what is left as block content, which is why the pair also counts Paragraph: the subsequent operation is the second half of the criterion, and 100 paragraphs against 100 paragraphs is what shows it matches. The earlier refusal said no reference table has block cells, which answers the wrong question -- the criterion asks for a reference PRODUCTION of this shape, not a reference table. The grid table is used rather than the multiline table because only the grid form is recognisable with ONE column: a multiline table establishes its columns from a SEGMENTED dash line, and a single unbroken dash run is a thematic break or a setext underline, so the one-column multiline table does not exist to be paired. Both sides use the zero-padded index, because a grid row must close its cell at the border's column and an index gaining a digit part way through would silently turn the rest of the document into a paragraph.

A LEADING table caption and a GFM table header line are the same production: a paragraph-shaped line already scanned, retroactively claimed by a table that a LATER line announces. GFM's delimiter row promotes the line above it into the table; the dialect's table promotes the `Table: ` line above it into the same table. The two units are line for line the same shape -- four lines, one of them a delimiter row, three carrying inlines, the first of those adopted by lookbehind -- and both sides build one table with three Text nodes per unit, which is the equality the pair rests on. That the dialect materialises the adopted line as a TableCaption owning its inlines where GFM materialises it as a header row owning a cell owning its inlines is node materialisation, which is never grounds to refuse. The pair is held by the ABSENCE of Paragraph on either side: both spellings degrade to a paragraph the moment the adoption stops being recognised, so a paragraph appearing anywhere in either document means some of it is no longer the construct being paired. This replaces a withdrawn proof that said neither grammar adopts a finished neighbouring block; the proof was written for the TRAILING form and wrongly applied to both.

A definition and a loose list item are the same production: a first line parsed as INLINE content, plus block content bound to it by indentation, under ONE node. The trees show it -- a Definition owns DefinitionTerm(inlines) and DefinitionBody(blocks) where a loose ListItem owns Paragraph(inlines) and the same blocks, and that the dialect materialises the two halves as owned groups where the list keeps flat children is node materialisation, which is never grounds to refuse a pair. This replaces a withdrawn proof that said CommonMark has no production grouping a preceding line's inlines with a following block under one node; a loose list item is exactly that. What differs is where the marker sits: a list item is recognised at its own first line, a definition promotes the PRECEDING line when `: ` arrives on the next, so it needs lookahead. That is the thing this pair measures, and it is not a reason to refuse -- GFM already promotes a paragraph by the delimiter row beneath it.

unpairable.proof: RE-DERIVED, because the first statement was the construct-not-production error and happened to survive it. Wrong version: CommonMark has no production that derives a binding from a node's own content. That invites the obvious counter -- a link reference definition also NORMALISES a string and registers it in a name table, which is the same subsequent operation, and it is exactly the reasoning that produced the discarded 1.27x pair. The real difference is in the production, not the operation: a link reference definition IS a binding declaration and builds no block; a derived anchor is a binding attached as a SIDE EFFECT to a block that carries inline content and exists independently of it. Neither reference grammar attaches a derived binding to a content-bearing block, so there is nothing of that shape to write. This also explains why the EXPLICIT anchor pairs and this does not: `#name#` declares, and a declaration is what a link reference definition is.

unpairable.production: a heading as the reference half -- CONTAMINATES Grammar and Shape, NOT same-job
unpairable.proof: WITHDRAWN AS STATED, and the correction runs the other way. The claim was that a heading can never be the reference half of a pair anywhere in this corpus, because this dialect derives an anchor on every heading including in plain CommonMark. The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow. Take the three numbers as the driver computes them: grammar = core/twinCore, shape = twinCore/twinCmark, sameJob = core/twinCmark. The anchor derivation lands in twinCore -- this parser's cost on the isomorph half -- and twinCore CANCELS out of sameJob, which is this parser on the DIALECT document over the REFERENCE on the isomorph. The dialect document has no headings and cmark derives no anchors, so sameJob is clean. What is contaminated is Grammar, whose denominator is inflated so it reads low, and Shape, whose numerator is inflated so it reads high. A heading isomorph therefore yields a valid same-job ratio -- the number the ranking sorts on -- and two numbers that must be suppressed.

The only proof here with the right SHAPE -- an exhaustive enumeration over both grammars rather than a claim about one construct -- and it is restated as one. An inline footnote is recognised mid-line, its body is parsed as INLINE content, and its node is hoisted out of the content tree into a document-owned side list. Enumerate every inline production of both grammars: code span, emphasis, strong, link, image, autolink, raw HTML, hard break, soft break, entity, text; plus GFM's strikethrough, autolink literal and footnote reference. Every one of them leaves its node where it was recognised. Hoisting exists in GFM only for the footnote DEFINITION, which is a block. So the enumeration is complete and the shape is absent from both grammars. NOTE the honest caveat: nine of the ten claims withdrawn today were single-construct assertions, and this one has not been attacked by anyone but its author.

openCandidates.whyTheEarlierProofWasWrong: Both the multiline and the grid table were refused because their cells hold BLOCK content and no reference table has block cells. That answers the wrong question: the criterion asks for a reference PRODUCTION of this shape, not a reference table. The grid half of that refusal is now a built pair -- a one-column grid cell against a loose list item, both a per-line positional cut whose remainder is parsed as blocks -- so the block-cell argument is settled and this entry is only about what the grid pair does not reach.
openCandidates.whatIsGenuinelyUnsettled: The multiline table cannot be reduced to one column the way the grid table can. It establishes its columns from a SEGMENTED dash line, and a single unbroken dash run is a thematic break or a setext underline, so there is no one-column multiline table to pair. That leaves its row production at K>=2: one line cut into K ranges at positions established by one earlier line. A reference container cuts each line ONCE, at a prefix, and K side-by-side containers are K productions rather than one. Whether the K-way cut pairs with anything, or whether the honest move is to pair at the CELL level and let the row-level slicing show up as the dialect side's extra, is the thing to decide.
openCandidates.status: OPEN -- to be built and tested, not asserted either way

openCandidates.whyTheEarlierProofWasWrong: Demoted without a specific counter-example, on the record rather than on the merits. Ten impossibility claims were re-examined today and ten fell or narrowed, every one of them a single-construct assertion written to close an item rather than to survive attack. This proof is of that kind and has not been re-derived, so it is not entitled to stand as a proof. Two of these are known to use the exact error: the container directive argues 'CommonMark's only fence opens a leaf', which compares constructs and not productions, and the headerless simple table argues from GFM's table requiring a header rather than from the row-and-cell production.
